text:
Seven people left OpenAI in late 2020 and founded Anthropic in January 2021. Tonight it prices the biggest IPO of the year, and each of the seven is suddenly worth about $18 billion. Forbes puts each founder's stake at $17.6 billion to $17.9 billion at the $74 midpoint of the $70-to-$78 range. That is the headline. The cast behind it is stranger than the money.

Dario Amodei, 43, the CEO, a biophysics PhD whose early work at Stanford Medicine was cancer research. His sister Daniela, 39, the president and board chair, a literature major who ran teams at Stripe. Tom Brown, 39, the chief compute officer, an MIT engineer who co-founded the dating app Grouper before leading GPT-3. Jack Clark, 37, the former Bloomberg tech reporter who now runs the Anthropic Institute. Jared Kaplan, 42, the chief science officer, a Harvard physicist who co-wrote the scaling laws. Sam McCandlish, 36, the chief architect, a Stanford physicist who orchestrates large-model training. Chris Olah, 34, the college dropout who studies why AI makes the choices it does. Two siblings, three PhDs, a journalist, a dropout.

The money is simpler than the people. Each founder holds about 240 million shares, roughly 1.4% of the company; together they own about 1.69 billion, close to 10%. At the $74 midpoint, the stake each keeps is worth $17.6 billion to $17.9 billion, and each sells 3,378,378 shares in the IPO for about $250 million more. It is paper wealth. The shares are locked up, and the founders have pledged 80% of their equity to charity.

The market is voting. Grey-market trading in Germany put Anthropic near €101, about 45% above the top of the range, demand is reported near seven times the shares on offer, and the Journal expects a price above $80. First trade is Thursday on Nasdaq under ANT. Red pen: the $18 billion is a Forbes estimate at the IPO midpoint, not cash, and Jack Clark is 37, not 38 as some versions say. Seven founders, one safety-first lab, all running it.

text:
🚨 2028 BOMBSHELL: IS RAND PAUL PREPARING TO CHALLENGE JD VANCE FOR PRESIDENT?

Senator Rand Paul is making some serious noise about the future of the Republican Party, and his latest comments are raising a major question: Is the Kentucky Republican laying the groundwork for another presidential campaign in 2028?

In a revealing interview with the Washington Examiner, Paul unloaded on Vice President JD Vance, the Trump administration's spending priorities, immigration enforcement tactics, tariffs, and what he believes has become a Republican Party that has completely abandoned its commitment to fiscal conservatism.

And he didn't exactly slam the door on running for president himself.

Paul specifically singled out Vance when discussing potential 2028 Republican contenders who could damage the party's future, arguing that the vice president belongs to a growing faction of populists who seemingly believe federal deficits don't matter.

That's a significant political shot at a man widely viewed as one of the leading potential contenders for the next Republican presidential nomination.

Paul warned that the federal government could add another $8 trillion to the national debt over four years, criticized proposals for hundreds of billions in additional military spending, and argued that Republicans have become just as irresponsible with taxpayer dollars as the Democrats they spent years attacking.

His message was unmistakable: Republicans cannot continue promising smaller government and fiscal responsibility while overseeing massive deficits and expanding federal spending.

But Paul's criticism went well beyond the national debt.

He also took aim at the administration's immigration enforcement tactics, calling for greater accountability following a deadly ICE operation in Texas. While reaffirming his support for border security and lawful immigration, Paul argued that enforcement agencies must be held accountable when serious questions arise about their actions.

He also blamed tariffs, rising consumer costs, and what he described as a disconnect between Republican leadership and everyday Americans for contributing to the party's disappointing midterm election results.

Perhaps his harshest assessment came when he suggested the GOP needs to acknowledge its failures, change its presentation, and bring in new leadership rather than simply doubling down on policies that voters rejected.

Now comes the interesting part.

When asked about his own political future and whether he might lead the Republican Party in a different direction, Paul refused to rule anything out.

"That's yet to be determined," he said.

He later joked that he would have to make a decision sometime before November 2028, while acknowledging that a serious presidential campaign would require an earlier commitment.

That is certainly not a presidential announcement, but it is far from a definitive no.

Remember, Rand Paul already ran for president in 2016. He has an established national profile, a loyal libertarian-leaning conservative following, and a political identity built around limited government, constitutional liberties, reducing federal spending, and opposing unnecessary foreign intervention.

A 2028 campaign could give him an opportunity to revive those arguments at a time when the Republican Party is debating what comes after Donald Trump.

Of course, Paul would face enormous challenges. President Trump's populist movement has fundamentally reshaped the GOP, and Paul's criticism of tariffs, military policy, and immigration enforcement could put him at odds with significant portions of the Republican primary electorate.

But that could also be exactly the political lane he is trying to establish.

Could 2028 become a battle between JD Vance's America First populism and Rand Paul's more traditional, limited-government conservatism?

text:
🚨TREV ALBERTS INFORMATION🚨

Let's go back to 2011.

Alberts was the athletic director at Nebraska-Omaha when the university eliminated its football and wrestling programs. The wrestling team had just won its THIRD consecutive Division II national championship when it learned the program was being eliminated.

Imagine winning a national championship and finding out hours later that your program is finished.

Now fast-forward to 2023.

An internal university memo raised serious concerns about financial oversight during much of Alberts' tenure at Nebraska-Omaha. It alleged a lack of fiscal discipline, questionable accounting practices, and potentially misleading financial information provided to donors and university leadership.

Those allegations were disputed by Nebraska leadership, and I'm not suggesting Alberts personally committed fraud. But the fact that these concerns were documented deserves attention.

Then there's his career trajectory.

He left Nebraska, his own alma mater, for Texas A&M in 2024.

He signed a lucrative contract extension at A&M.

Now, less than three years after arriving in College Station, he's leaving for Michigan, with the university reportedly covering a $4 million buyout.

I'll give him credit for the $515 million multimedia rights deal at Texas A&M. That's impressive. He also hired Matt Rhule at Nebraska.

But Michigan just went through an absolute circus under Warde Manuel. We've dealt with administrative dysfunction, embarrassing scandals, and a football program that has completely lost its direction.

The last thing Michigan needs is another athletic director whose leadership becomes a controversy of its own.

I'm not saying Alberts is going to fail. I'm saying his résumé deserves considerably more scrutiny than simply celebrating Michigan stealing an athletic director from the SEC.

Michigan needs stability, accountability, and somebody who actually intends to build something here for the long term.

After everything this university has gone through, I don't think that's asking too much.

Mackinac County, Michigan. The Michigan State Police (MSP) St. Ignace Post is proud to announce the promotion of Sam Eckola from trooper to sergeant.

Sergeant Eckola grew up in the Upper Peninsula, and he earned a bachelor’s degree in Criminal Justice from Lake Superior State University. Sergeant Eckola enlisted with the MSP in June 2017 as a member of the 133rd Trooper Recruit School. Upon graduation, he was assigned to the St. Ignace Post, where he began his career as a trooper.

Sergeant Eckola also served as a detective trooper with the Upper Peninsula Substance Enforcement Team (UPSET), dedicating several years to combating illegal drug activity in the Upper Peninsula. Sergeant Eckola has received the department’s Cpl. Samuel A. Mapes Award multiple times, which recognizes high performing troopers for outstanding performance and commitment to excellence in proactive criminal patrol and criminal investigations.

Sergeant Eckola will help oversee daily operations at the St. Ignace Post and support troopers as they work with other local law enforcement to serve communities throughout Mackinac County.

The MSP St. Ignace Post congratulates Sergeant Eckola on his promotion and looks forward to his continued commitment to serving the people of Mackinac County.
